source.title: An Active-Bottleneck Mechanism for Weak-to-Strong Generalization

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether a student trained on a teacher's pseudo-labels can outperform the teacher, but uses theoretical and simulated ridgeless regression with expected-risk gain rather than pretrained-model fine-tuning and PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper's own two-stage risk results bear on the claim. Related-work results attributed to other papers, including Busbridge et al., are cited background and are not recorded as rows. The study does not compute Burns et al.'s PGR or compare against a strong model trained on true labels.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper with Monte Carlo checks. In two-stage ridgeless linear and random-feature regression, it derives and simulates when a student trained only on a teacher's pseudo-labels has lower population risk than the teacher (W2SG = RT − RS > 0). These are the paper's own results on whether, and under what conditions, a student beats its supervisor. They bear mainly on V5, and on V1 and V3 in the random-feature case, where the student can be wider than the teacher. No PGR, pretrained models or true-label ceiling are used.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a finite Stage-II resource held in an intermediate range yields weak-to-strong improvement at full ridgeless convergence, with no early stopping or explicit regularization, and in Case I with no capacity advantage. In Case II, either m or NS can be the active bottleneck; the non-bottleneck resource can be increased freely. A positive region requires the student to be wider than the teacher, but width alone does not suffice. They conjecture the principle extends to nonlinear and LLM-scale settings, citing Busbridge et al.'s non-monotone distillation results.
record.recipe_differences: The original studies fine-tuning of pretrained models on weak-model labels and measures PGR. This paper studies minimum-norm ridgeless linear and random-feature regression, measures expected population-risk gain, and uses theoretical analysis plus Monte Carlo simulation rather than pretrained-model fine-tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: The sign and extent of improvement vary with spectral exponent α, noise level σ², fixed versus proportional or sparse-growing m, pseudo-sample ratio, student feature width, signal fraction, teacher mismatch, and which Stage-II resource is the bottleneck.

fits_no_version.finding: In Case I, a student with exactly the teacher's hypothesis class and training rule beats the teacher depending only on the number of pseudo-labels m and the spectral decay. The improving set can be one interval, all m < p, or two disjoint windows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Self-distillation with equal capacity can beat the teacher through a finite pseudo-label bottleneck; the effect of pseudo-label count is non-monotone.

record.problems: The experiments are Monte Carlo simulations of theoretical regression models, not pretrained-model evaluations. Reported plots include confidence bands but the text does not provide their bounds. The fixed-m and sparse-growing deterministic-equivalent analyses rely on continuation assumptions explicitly stated by the paper; several phase results apply only to specified covariance and asymptotic regimes.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix derivations and duplicate formulations of the phase results are not separate outcomes from the main theorem rows. Cited findings from other work are excluded. The study reports no separate result for the vision, method-gains, or distribution-shift versions.

untested.parts: PGR, pretrained language models, true-label strong ceiling, and classification tasks. Case I has no stronger student at all.
Entire version: no auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling or loss variants.
NLP, chess and reward-modelling tasks, and pretrained-model representations. Supervisor size enters only through ρT in the theory and is not swept in the simulations.
Entire version: no distribution shift, exploitation or error-similarity analysis.
Students and supervisors outside linear and random-feature regression. Covariances other than power-law or two-block. α > 1+√2 and Case II boundary cases are only partially resolved.
Entire version: no vision or other modality.

missing.what: Case I, α=1.8, σ²=2: gain positive throughout all three regimes, with a strongly non-monotone finite-p curve
Any positive-W2SG region in Case II forces ρS > ϑ+ΛT > ρT: the student must be wider than the teacher, but this is not sufficient
Feature-bottleneck positive region as a bounded interval in ρS, and sample-bottleneck region as a half-line in ρS
Interpolation singularity: when |m−NS| ≤ 1 and min(m, NS) < p, student risk is infinite and W2SG = −∞
Unique fixed-m transition for small noise and its location; critical α=2 tail-noise threshold
missing.locator: Theorem A.38, Corollaries A.39 and A.42

missing.what: Finite-size convergence of finite-p curves toward the fixed-m and proportional limits for p in {200, 400, 800, 1000}
Joint teacher–student criticality near the signal dimension: sample branch stays negative, while the feature branch can stay positive

record.verdict_notes: This is a theory paper. The key judgment is that Case I (same hypothesis class) is not a strong-student setup, so its rows are relinked to V5 only, and the finding is also recorded under fits_no_version. Case II rows bear on V1 and V3 because the student can have more random features than the teacher. The Case II teacher is a noiseless population-risk minimiser, so its error is pure approximation bias. The T2 tranche is borderline; T5 would also be defensible, since the results argue that student improvement is conditional rather than general.

versions.untested_parts: Tests student-versus-teacher improvement using expected population-risk gain, not PGR; does not use pretrained language models or true-label-trained strong-model ceilings.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling of weak supervisors, or comparison of loss variants.

Studies linear and random-feature regression, spectral decay, pseudo-sample size, and feature width; does not test NLP, chess, reward modelling, language-model size, or representation predictors in pretrained models.
Does not test distribution shift, weak-supervisor checkability, or whether shared error patterns shrink gains.
Derives model-specific conditions for the two regression settings, not general conditions for arbitrary students and supervisors.
No vision or other non-language modality experiment.

rows.subject: Case I: ridgeless regression
rows.size_stated: feature dimension p; m and p grow proportionally
rows.stage_stated: both stages ridgeless and trained to convergence
rows.operation_detail: Train the student by minimum-norm regression on fresh inputs labeled by the teacher; evaluate expected population-risk gain W2SG = RT − RS.
rows.value: W2SGDE > 0 for every proportional m < p
rows.note: Theoretical result for identical teacher and student hypothesis classes; the student improves throughout the stated proportional regime.
rows.check: Case I teacher and student share one hypothesis class, so the student is not a stronger model. This does not bear on V1 (a strong model on weak labels) or on V3's supervisor/student size axis. It is a V5 condition result.

rows.size_stated: feature dimension p; m and p grow proportionally
rows.stage_stated: both stages ridgeless and trained to convergence
rows.operation_detail: Vary the proportional Stage-II sample ratio and evaluate the deterministic-equivalent risk gain.
rows.value: There is a unique critical ϕm,crit; W2SGDE > 0 iff ϕm < ϕm,crit, equivalently m > mcritFP(p) ∼ p/ϕm,crit.
rows.note: Improvement holds only on one side of a sample-ratio threshold; it is not guaranteed for every proportional m.
rows.check: Same-capacity Case I, so V5 only. Positive only for m above a Θ(p) critical ratio.

rows.operation_detail: Analyze fixed-m limiting risk gain as a function of pseudo-sample count.

rows.note: The result establishes a sign change but does not establish uniqueness at this noise level.
rows.check: Same-capacity Case I, so V5 only. Relies on the paper's fixed-m deterministic-equivalent continuation assumption (A.24).

rows.subject: Case I: ridgeless regression
rows.stage_stated: both stages ridgeless and trained to convergence
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate the sparse-growing Stage-II deterministic-equivalent gain.
rows.value: W2SGDE → (2 − α)σ²γT/(1 − γT): positive for 1 < α < 2, zero for α = 2, and negative for α > 2.

rows.subject: Case II: random-feature regression
rows.size_stated: m, NS, NT and p grow proportionally
rows.operation_detail: Vary the Stage-II resource ratios relative to the signal fraction and evaluate the risk gain.
rows.note: If either student resource is below the signal fraction, the student fails to improve on the teacher.
rows.check: Includes configurations where the student is wider than the teacher (ρS > ρT) but m is below the signal fraction. The gain is still negative.

rows.subject: Case II: random-feature regression
rows.size_stated: m, NS, NT and p grow proportionally
rows.operation_detail: Sweep pseudo-sample size while the sample count is the scarcer Stage-II resource.
rows.value: W2SGDE > 0 iff ρm lies in the stated bounded interval, when its discriminant is positive; otherwise this branch has no positive region.
rows.note: The positive interval requires the sample-bottleneck branch and may be empty.

rows.subject: Case II: random-feature regression
rows.size_stated: m, NS, NT and p grow proportionally
rows.operation_detail: Vary student feature width while pseudo-sample size is not the scarcer Stage-II resource.
rows.value: W2SGDE > 0 iff ρS − ϑ > ΛT and ρm > 2ρS(ρS − ϑ)/(ρS − ϑ − ΛT).
rows.note: Once the feature bottleneck meets its condition, sufficiently many pseudo-labels yield improvement.

rows.subject: Case II: random-feature regression

rows.note: The paper's no-bottleneck condition makes the student reproduce the teacher exactly.
rows.check: The student can have more features than the teacher here, yet exactly reproduces it.

statements.correction: Theorem 5.4(ii): bounded positive interval in ρm on the sample-bottleneck branch. Theorem 5.4(iii): positive half-line in ρm on the feature-bottleneck branch when ρS − ϑ > ΛT. Corollary 5.6: bounded interval in ρS on the feature branch and positive half-line on the sample branch.
statements.problem: The negative and zero-gain claims are correct, but positivity is not confined globally to bounded windows.

statements.correction: Case II: bounded interval in m when m is the bottleneck; sufficiently large m improves performance when NS is the bottleneck and meets its threshold. At fixed m, the corresponding width scan has a bounded feature-bottleneck interval and may have a sample-bottleneck positive half-line.
statements.problem: The window description omits the positive half-lines available when the scanned resource is not the bottleneck.

statements.correction: Corollary 5.6(i): bounded positive interval in ρS while ρS < min{1, ρm}. Corollary 5.6(ii): positive half-line at larger ρS when its conditions hold. Section 6.2.1 explicitly reports positivity resuming. More pseudo-labels can remove the gain on the sample-bottleneck branch.
statements.problem: The bounded width interval applies only to the feature-bottleneck branch; Figure 4 also shows positivity returning at larger width. Non-monotone dependence supports V3's descriptive claim.

statements.correction: For 2 < α ≤ 1 + √2 in the proportional regime, mcrit ∼ p/ϕm,crit = Θ(p), and improvement holds for mcrit < m < p. The critical ratio mcrit/p is constant order. For 1 < α ≤ 2, every fixed proportional ratio 0 < m/p < 1 gives positive limiting gain.
statements.problem: Θ(p) describes the critical sample count, not the ratio; the Case I threshold statement needs its spectral regime.

statements.correction: Theorem 4.4(a)(ii): proportional threshold for 2 < α ≤ 1 + √2. Theorem 4.4(a)(i): positive gain at every proportional m < p for 1 < α ≤ 2. Theorem A.35: negative near m = 1 for 1 < α < 2 and 0 < σ² < σc². Proposition 4.1: zero gain for m ≥ p.
statements.problem: The critical proportional threshold is not universal across Case I, and negative gain near m = 1 requires the stated small-noise condition.
